Based on the provided healthcare Q&A matches, it appears that the consensus among country experts in Europe is that patient and graft survival rates are equivalent when living-related kidney transplants are performed from older donors to younger recipients. However, renal function is generally better in younger donors.

Therefore, the short- and long-term outcomes after Living-Related Liver Transplantation (LR LT) did not differ significantly between two treatment options: LR T with waiting list cadaveric organs versus Short-Term Living-Related Liver Transplantation with selected use of imaging. To avoid potential risks for the donor in LR LT, Selective Living-Related Liver Transplantation with ultrasonography representation represents an alternative approach.

The available evidence suggests that LR LT provides a viable solution for urgent cases or situations where a cadaveric graft cannot be found in time or when the optimal transplantation timing is crucial. On the other hand, LR T has been shown to provide a suitable option for patients who require immediate liver transplantation due to a donor shortage.

In summary, while there are no definitive conclusions that living-related liver transplantation in children should not occur anymore, selective Living-Related Liver Transplantation with ultrasonography representation appears as an alternative approach that may offer some benefits over waiting list cadaveric organs alone. However, more research is needed to fully understand the risks and benefits of this option and its implications on patient outcomes and health care practices in Europe.
